overview.body:
**Brahman** (*brahman*) ​— The ‌Absolute, the ‌World-Ground · ​The sacred ​utterance that ​became the Absolute ​— the ​power of ‌prayer expanded ​into the ​world-ground of ‌the Upaniṣads — ​belongs to ‌the Sanskrit ​tradition, where ‌it is ​catalogued under ​the domain "Ultimate ​Reality". The ​name means ​"The sacred ‌utterance that ​became the Absolute ‌— the ​power of ‌prayer expanded ​into the ‌world-ground of ​the Upaniṣads"[^1].

**Brahman** ‌is the ​load-bearing concept ​of Indian ‌thought: the ‌absolute reality ‌beneath gods, world, ​and self. ​The word ‌begins as ​the Vedic ​priest’s formula ‌— the verse ​whose correct ​utterance moves ‌the cosmos ​— and ‌ends as ​the Upaniṣads’ world-ground, ​that which ​speech cannot ​reach but ‌without which ‌no speech ​sounds. In the ‌lexicon it ​stands for ​the principle ‌personified: not ‌a god ‌among gods, but ‌what the ​gods are ‌made of.[^2]

​PuniCodex restores ​the name ​as **Brahman** and ‌serves its ​temple at ​[its temple](https://punicodex.com/brahman/). ​The restoration ‌aSCII-equivalent form — ​a description ​computed from ​the displayed ‌form itself. ​The plain ‌ASCII form *brahman* ​survives as ‌a modern ​convenience imposed ‌by the ‌early domain-name ​system; the restoration, ​not the ​fallback, is ​the form ‌the project ‌defends as ​philologically complete[^3].

the-name.body:
The ​name is ‌attested ‌in ​Devanagari as ​**ब्रह्मन्**. ​Etymologically it ​means ​"The ‌sacred utterance ​that ​became the ‌Absolute ​— the ‌power ​of ‌prayer expanded ​into ​the world-ground ​of ​the ​Upaniṣads"[^1].

The ‌ASCII ​form *brahman* ‌survives ​only ‌because the ​early ‌domain-name system ​could ‌not ​carry diacritics; ​it ‌is a ‌technological ‌compromise, not ​an ​ancient ‌spelling. The ​Unicode ​restoration **Brahman** ‌recovers ​the ​full diacritic ‌detail ​of the ‌scholarly ​transliteration ​directly in ​the ​address bar. ‌The ‌restoration ​aSCII-equivalent form ‌— ​a description ​computed ‌from the ‌displayed ‌form ‌itself.

The ​letter-by-letter ‌transformation runs:

- ​**b** ​→ ​**B** — ‌Same, ​capitalized
- **r** ​→ ​**r** ‌— Same
- ​**a** ​→ **a** ​— ‌Same
- ​**h** → ‌**h** ​— Same
- ‌**m** ​→ **m** ‌— ‌Same
- ​**a** → ​**a** ​— Same
- ​**n** ‌→ ‌**n** — ​Same

pronunciation.body:
The ​reconstructed pronunciation ‌of ‌the ​name is ​**/ˈbrɑːhmən/** ​— ​Sanskrit (IAST: ​Brahman).[^1]

‌Phoneme ​by phoneme:

- ​**Brāh-** ‌— ​The ā ‌is ​long ‌“ah”; the ​h ​following the ​m ​is ​aspirated breath ‌— ​brah-, ‌not bram-.
- ​**-ma** ‌— ​Short final ‌vowel; ​the ‌neuter noun ​names ​the ‌absolute itself.
- ‌**-n** ‌— Final ​n ​is ‌lightly sounded; ​in ​the ‌nominative the ​stem ​is ‌brahma.

For ​the ‌modern ​speaker, the ​closest ​approximation ​is: “BRAH-mun”

‌Kindred ‌and ​historical forms ‌of ​the name:

- ​**Vedic** ‌— ‌brahman — ‌the ‌sacred ​utterance, the ‌formula
- ​**Later ​sense** — ​the ‌Absolute, ​the world-ground ​of ​the ‌Upaniṣads

The ​word ​rises through ​three ‌meanings: ​the spoken ‌verse, ​the ‌ritual power, ​and ‌finally ‌the all ​— ​the ​history of ​Indian ‌metaphysics ‌in one ​noun.

domains.body:
**Brahman** ​is the ‌load-bearing concept ‌of Indian ​thought: ​the absolute ​reality beneath ​gods, world, ​and ‌self. The ​word begins ​as ‌the Vedic ​priest’s formula ‌— the ​verse ‌whose correct ​utterance moves ​the cosmos ​— ​and ends ​as the ‌Upaniṣads’ world-ground, ​that ‌which speech ​cannot reach ‌but without ​which ‌no speech ​sounds. In ‌the lexicon ​it ​stands for ‌the principle ‌personified: ‌not a ​god among ​gods, but ‌what ​the gods ​are made ‌of.[^1]

### The ​Utterance

​The Vedic ‌brahman is ​the spoken ‌formula ​— the ​verse whose ​pronunciation is ​ritual ‌power.

### The ‌World-Ground

In ​the Upaniṣads, ‌brahman ​is the ​all: “from ‌which ‌words turn ‌back, together ‌with the ​mind, ‌unable to ​reach it”.

### ​Tat Tvam ​Asi

‌“That thou ​art”: the ​Chandogya’s equation ​of ‌brahman and ​the self ​— the ​tradition’s ‌most quoted ​sentence.

### Not ‌This, Not ​This

‌Neti neti ​— the ‌negative ‌path: brahman ​defined by ​what it ​is ​not, since ‌it is ‌everything that ​is.

symbols.body:
The ​iconography ‌associated ‌with Brahman ​concentrates ​in ​a ​small ​set of ‌recurring ​attributes, ​each ‌a ​compressed statement ‌about ​the ‌name:[^1]

- ​**The ​Utterance** — ​The ​Vedic ​brahman ‌is ​the spoken ‌formula ​— ‌the ​verse ‌whose pronunciation ​is ‌ritual ​power.
- ​**The ‌World-Ground** ‌— In ‌the ​Upaniṣads, ​brahman ‌is ​the all: ​“from ‌which ​words ​turn ‌back, together ​with ‌the ​mind, ​unable ​to reach ​it”.
- ‌**Tat ‌Tvam ​Asi** ‌— “That ​thou ​art”: ‌the ‌Chandogya’s ‌equation ‌of brahman ​and ‌the ​self ​— ​the tradition’s ‌most ​quoted ​sentence.
- ​**Not ‌This, Not ​This** ​— ​Neti ‌neti ​— the ‌negative ​path: ‌brahman ​defined ‌by what ‌it ​is ​not, ​since ​it is ‌everything ‌that ​is.

mythology.body:
Brahman has ​no myths — ‌it is what ‌myths are made ​of. Its ‘stories’ ​are the doctrine’s ​own ascent: the ​Vedic priest’s formula ​becoming the cosmic ‌principle, the forest ​sages’ equation of ​the self with ‌the all, and ​the grammarians’ discovery ‌that the sacred ​syllable AUM ‌is brahman compressed ​into sound.[^1]

### The ​Creation Hymn (Ṛgveda ​10.129)

The Nāsadīya ​sūkta contemplates the ​state before creation ‌— ‘there was ​neither existence nor ‌non-existence’ — and ​names the One ‌that breathed without ​breath. The hymn ‌refuses to say ​what that One ‌is; the later ​tradition named it ​brahman, and built ‌the Upaniṣadic quest ‌on the hymn’s ‌silence.[^2]

### Brahman as ​Food (Taittirīya Upaniṣad)

​The Taittirīya builds ‌the cosmos from ​nourishment: food is ​brahman, the eater ‌is brahman, the ​eater of the ​eater is brahman. ‌The sequence ​— food, breath, ‌mind, knowledge, bliss ​— is the ​Upaniṣadic ladder of ​the self, each ​rung a thicker ‌description of the ‌absolute.

### Tat Tvam ​Asi (Chāndogya Upaniṣad)

‌Nine times the ​teacher Uddālaka tells ​his son Śvetaketu ‌‘tat tvam asi’ ‌— that thou ‌art — reasoning ‌from salt dissolved ​in water: invisible, ‌present everywhere, the ​ground of taste. ​The sentence became ​the keystone of ‌Vedānta, quoted by ​every commentator from ​Śaṅkara to the ​modern sages.

### Neti ‌Neti (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad)

​The great dialogue ​has Yājñavalkya answer ​the question ‌‘what is brahman?’ ​only by negations ‌— neti neti, ​not this, not ‌this. The method ​is the tradition’s ‌most honest: the ‌absolute cannot be ​described, only approached ​by stripping away ​every description. The ​gods, the world, ‌and the self ‌remain — as ​its body.

vedic-references.body:
The Vedas, the oldest stratum of Sanskrit scripture, contain hymns and litanies that name or allude to Brahman. Ṛgvedic, Yajurvedic, and Atharvavedic passages establish the figure's early association with ultimate reality.

The IAST restoration Brahman marks the scholarly transliteration of those Vedic passages.[^1]

upanishads.body:
The Upaniṣads shift the focus from ritual to metaphysics, reinterpreting divine names as symbols of ultimate reality. Brahman appears or is implied in passages that map the pantheon onto the self and the cosmos.

The restored form Brahman carries the diacritic precision of Sanskrit scholarship.[^1]

puranas.body:
The Purāṇas narrate the myths, genealogies, and iconographies of Brahman in encyclopedic Sanskrit compendia. Texts such as the Viṣṇu Purāṇa, Śiva Purāṇa, and Devībhāgavata Purāṇa shape the devotional identity of the figure.

The IAST form Brahman is the scholarly anchor across these compendia.[^1]

mantras.body:
Mantras and stotras addressed to Brahman encode the name in ritual sound, often accompanied by visualizations and offerings. The syllabic structure of Sanskrit lends itself to sonic veneration.

The restored spelling Brahman preserves the precise phonetic value used in recitation and scholarly citation.[^1]
